deep.reconstruction:
Setting, inferred from neighbouring pages. Grothendieck is studying a 2-dimensional cell structure X attached to systems of pseudo-lines; the next page speaks of (X, K, S_K), a graph L ⊂ X, and 'axes cartésiens'. A 2-face F of X has a boundary ∂F subdivided into 'grandes cellules' (big cells, i.e. closed arcs between distinguished vertices) and finer 'petites cellules'. To each cell α of ∂F a sign ε_F(α) = ±1 is attached. These are plausibly orientation or chirotope-type signs of the configurations involved. The vertices of order 4 adjacent to F form an arc V_F, the 'green' vertices. For a big cell a of ∂F, F' = σ_a(F) is the face adjacent to F across a; σ_a is the identification or crossing map.

Aim. Use the positions of the 'critical arcs' to compute the signs ε_{F'} from the signs ε_F.

Proposition.
(a) Let A = A_{F,a} be the union of the big cells α of ∂F such that σ_a(α) is again a big cell of F'. Then A is an arc of ∂F. Let B be the complementary arc. On B one compares two subdivisions: into big cells of F (light-green vertices) and into big cells of F' (dark-green vertices). The edge counts n_a(F), n_a(F') involved lie between 3 and 5. Only three combinatorial types occur, listed as (3,2), (3,3), (3,4); these are cases 1°, 2°, 3°. In each case it is the 'special' face that carries 3 arcs, which identifies it in cases 1° and 3°.
(b) For a cell α ⊂ A with α ≠ a, ε_{F'}(α) = ε_F(α). For α = a, the sign flips: ε_{F'}(a) = −ε_F(a).
(c) The margin figures enumerate the three configurations on B. Each shows an arc u…x…r…(s)…y…v. Big-cell brackets for one face carry +1 and the ones for the other carry −1 (one −1 in case 2°, two in case 3°), with the inherited signs ε_1, ε_2 at the ends.

Role of the result (next page).
- Corollary 1: the sign distribution for F determines the one for F'.
- Corollary 2: by connectedness of X, the signs for one face determine the signs for all faces.
- This would give an intrinsic description of the signs from the combinatorial structure alone, without coordinates. Exceptional ('suprapolar'?) faces still have to be treated separately.

In modern terms, this is a local wall-crossing or propagation rule. Crossing the cell a flips exactly one sign and preserves the signs along the shared arc A. This is analogous to a triangle flip (mutation) in a pseudoline arrangement changing exactly one chirotope value, combined with connectivity of the flip graph (Ringel) to propagate an orientation globally.
errors: The text says the edge numbers are 'compris entre 3 et 5'. The listed pairs (3,2), (3,3), (3,4) have second entries 2–4. Either the pairs record something else (e.g. counts on B only), or the range/list is slightly inconsistent. The intended meaning is unclear.
The proposition is admittedly verified only for non-exceptional faces; the next page says exceptional faces must still be examined separately. This is a gap acknowledged by the author.
Part (a), 'A is an arc', is asserted without proof on this page. The case enumeration in (c) is given only by pictures.

ideas.what: Signs attached to boundary cells of the faces of a cell complex of pseudoline configurations, flipping exactly at the crossed cell and preserved on the common arc.
ideas.modern_name: Local sign change under mutation/triangle flip (chirotope change under mutation in rank-3 oriented matroids); wall-crossing rule
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ringel (1956) for flip connectivity; Bland–Las Vergnas, Folkman–Lawrence (1978) for oriented matroids/chirotopes

ideas.what: Classification of how big-cell subdivisions of adjacent faces F, F' differ on the complementary arc B: three types (3,2), (3,3), (3,4), with a distinguished 'special' face carrying 3 arcs.
ideas.modern_name: Local combinatorics of adjacent cells in a cell complex of pseudoline arrangements (cf. higher Bruhat orders / zonotopal tilings)
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure (cf. Manin–Schechtman 1989, Ziegler 1993 for higher Bruhat orders)

ideas.what: Global determination of all signs from the signs on one face by connectedness of X; aim of a coordinate-free description of the signs.
ideas.modern_name: Propagation of an orientation/chirotope along a connected flip graph; intrinsic (axiomatic) orientation
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folkman–Lawrence, Bland–Las Vergnas (oriented matroid axiomatics); Goodman–Pollack (allowable sequences)

missed.claim: Grothendieck sets out to recover all signs ε intrinsically from the combinatorial structure (X, K, S_K) via a local 3-case crossing rule plus connectedness, without coordinates. He leaves exceptional faces untreated. This is a sketch of a combinatorial orientation theory on his complex of pseudoline configurations.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest unless the complex X is identified. It resembles known material (mutations, higher Bruhat orders), so novelty is doubtful. It documents Grothendieck independently rediscovering oriented-matroid-style sign propagation in 1983–84.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a local technical lemma in an unpublished study of pseudoline systems. The underlying principle — one sign flips across a wall, the others are preserved, and connectedness propagates the signs — is standard in oriented matroid theory. The specific 3-case classification is unpublished, but it is unlikely to surprise a specialist.
